candidates.attacker_control: The set of JobProperty objects passed to the step is fully controlled by whoever authors the Pipeline script that executes. In a multibranch project the executed script is taken from the trusted revision (SCMBinder.java:101-105, ReadTrustedStep.java:166-176); for an ordinary branch head the trusted revision equals the branch head, so a user with write access to any branch (but without Jenkins Item.CONFIGURE permission on the generated job) can supply a Jenkinsfile invoking `properties([...])`. In standalone Pipeline jobs, the script author controls the arguments as well. The HTTP form path (newInstance, lines 187-207) takes key/value JSON from the request, including the class name of the JobProperty to instantiate.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the executed Pipeline normally comes from the SCM trusted revision, so the script author is not necessarily an arbitrary unprivileged user (SCMBinder.java:101-105; ReadTrustedStep.java:176-177); checked that isApplicable() is enforced for the job class (JobPropertyStep.java:126-128); checked that BranchJobProperty is explicitly preserved rather than removed (lines 132-137); searched the whole repository for `checkPermission` (zero matches, confirming no authorization gate exists anywhere, but also meaning this may be a deliberate design in which trust is delegated to the Jenkinsfile revision rather than to request permissions); noted that the step is an intentional upstream feature (`Set job properties`), so a missing-permission-check finding is a design/authorization gap hypothesis, not a demonstrated exploit.
candidates.impact: A Pipeline author without Item.CONFIGURE can persistently modify a job's property set (add properties and remove any property whose descriptor id was recorded by a prior `properties` invocation). Where the installed property types can influence authorization, triggers, retention or build availability, this is a plausible privilege-escalation / job-configuration-integrity issue; it also defeats the explicit job-ACL denial in BranchJobProperty.decorateACL for multibranch branch projects. Severity depends on which JobProperty implementations are installed and reachable.
candidates.prerequisites: Ability to run a Pipeline containing the `properties` step (branch-write access in a multibranch project, or the ability to author/execute a Pipeline script); at least one registered JobPropertyDescriptor whose isApplicable(WorkflowJob.class) returns true and whose construction succeeds. Impact is greatest where the installed JobProperty types carry security or configuration semantics (for example a job-level authorization matrix property - note matrix-auth appears as a test dependency in pom.xml lines 197-201 - or trigger/retention/durability properties). No confirmation is available that such permission-granting property classes can be constructed/serialized from a sandboxed script without script approval.
candidates.root_cause: JobPropertyStep.Execution.run obtains the job from the build and writes the step-supplied JobProperty list into it via job.addProperty()/job.removeProperty() without checking any permission (the entire repository contains no checkPermission call). The only guard is JobPropertyDescriptor.isApplicable(job.getClass()) (line 126). Because the mutation goes through the Job object rather than the HTTP configuration surface, it is not subject to the ACLs that normally protect job configuration; specifically, BranchJobProperty.decorateACL() deliberately returns false for Item.CONFIGURE on branch projects (and Item.DELETE on non-dead branches), yet the step can still re-write the very property list of such a job. The descriptor's newInstance (lines 187-207) additionally resolves the class name from the submitted propertiesMap keys and calls d.newInstance(req, more) for any registered JobPropertyDescriptor, so the property set is fully request-/script-controlled.
candidates.title: `properties` step (JobPropertyStep) configures job properties without any authorization check, bypassing job ACL restrictions on multibranch branch projects
candidates.trace: Build starts (script from trusted revision; SCMBinder.java:105,135) -> Jenkinsfile executes `properties([...])` -> JobPropertyStep.Execution.run (JobPropertyStep.java:98) -> isApplicable loop (lines 125-129) -> properties recorded by the previous run's JobPropertyTrackerAction are removed and new ones added (lines 130-152) -> JobPropertyTrackerAction replaced (line 154) -> job configuration is durably modified although no Item.CONFIGURE check occurred anywhere in this path.
candidates.unverified: Could not verify how the surrounding Jenkins core/step API decides which principals may execute Pipeline steps, whether the `properties` step is usable in sandboxed scripts or restricted by ScriptApproval for the classes involved, whether a given JobProperty (e.g. an authorization-matrix property) can actually be instantiated and applied to confer privilege, or whether upstream later added a permission check. No build, test, scanner, or runtime execution was performed; the finding rests on source text plus the explicit Item.CONFIGURE denial in BranchJobProperty.decorateACL.
candidates.weakness_type: Missing authorization check (CWE-862) enabling privilege escalation via job-configuration mutation

coverage_summary: Scope: 34 source files in the assigned tree (13 Java, 21 non-Java: pom/CI/metadata, resource help HTML and Messages properties). P1 relation index reports 34/34 files indexed, 0 omitted/parse errors, Java-only syntax parsing, 173 symbols/427 call sites (394 unresolved), no control-flow or data-flow, no semantic resolution, Spring annotation candidates unverified. I read all 13 Java files in full and searched the tree for permission checks, trust checks, file reads, class loading, and SCM child access. Non-Java files (help pages, Messages bundles, CI/dependabot configs, README, .mvn/extensions.xml) were skimmed only for security-relevant hints; no test sources exist in the snapshot, so no test-derived evidence was available. No build, test, or dynamic analysis was run.
limitations: All findings are static; the P1 index explicitly disclaims control/data-flow, semantic resolution, runtime reachability, and exploitability proof, and 394 call sites were unresolved.

Key trust/authorization behavior lives in dependencies not present in the snapshot (Jenkins core step engine and ACL classes, workflow-job/workflow-cps, scm-api/branch-api, optionals such as matrix-auth), so the actual privilege model of Pipeline steps and which JobProperty classes are constructible/effective could not be verified.
No test sources, git history, advisory metadata, or patch information are available in the snapshot; the candidate was not compared against any known fix and is not runtime-confirmed.
Whether the `properties` step is reachable in sandboxed scripts without script approval, and whether any installed JobProperty can confer permissions, remain unverified and determine the real impact.
Resource/help HTML and localization files were not exhaustively reviewed for XSS/localization issues, and the CI workflow file was only skimmed.

rejected_leads.lead: ReadTrustedStep standalone-SCM path (lines 95-116) reads the requested path from SCMFileSystem with no trust check and no workspace-contained path validation
rejected_leads.reason: Intended behavior documented in the class comment and CHANGELOG (JENKINS-31386): in a standalone 'Pipeline from SCM' job the whole (trusted) Jenkinsfile already originates from that same SCM, so readTrusted adds no trust boundary there; the heavyweight paths do enforce the workspace containment check at lines 135-138.

rejected_leads.lead: ReadTrustedStep trust comparison can dereference a null untrustedFile/content (line 212) when a file is absent from one revision
rejected_leads.reason: This produces a NullPointerException/build failure, i.e. fails closed, not a trust-check bypass; no attacker-controlled path was found that reaches a comparison of equal values across different revisions.

rejected_leads.lead: ResolveScmStep.DescriptorImpl.newInstance binds an arbitrary SCMSource class from request JSON (line 192-194, src.put("id", "_"); req.bindJSON(SCMSource.class, src))
rejected_leads.reason: The method only constructs a step object used for snippet generation / form binding; no source evidence that the bound SCM is executed or that credentials are resolved at binding time, and access to the descriptor endpoint presupposes job read/snippet access. Unconfirmed and lower impact than the JobPropertyStep lead.

rejected_leads.lead: JobPropertyStep.DescriptorImpl.newInstance loads a class named by the request key via the webapp classloader and calls JobPropertyDescriptor.newInstance (lines 187-207)
rejected_leads.reason: Class loading is constrained by asSubclass(JobProperty.class) and getDescriptorOrDie, and this mirrors the standard Stapler configuration-binding trust level; no evidence of an escape beyond the same JobProperty instantiation that the runtime step already permits (treated as part of the single candidate's root cause rather than a separate finding).

rejected_leads.lead: SCMBinder only logs a warning (WarningNote + message) instead of aborting when the Jenkinsfile differs at the untrusted revision (lines 116-134)
rejected_leads.reason: Explicitly intentional in this revision (comment 'TODO JENKINS-45970 consider aborting instead, at least optionally'; CHANGELOG 2.21 describes the warning behavior); the trusted-revision script is still the one executed.

rejected_leads.lead: BranchJobProperty.decorateACL uses ACL.SYSTEM.equals(a) to detect system authentication (line 70)
rejected_leads.reason: The type/equality semantics of hudson.security.ACL.SYSTEM live in a dependency outside the snapshot and could not be verified here; the surrounding logic (denying Item.CONFIGURE and non-dead Item.DELETE) is coherent and consistent with upstream intent, so this is not a supportable finding.

summary: Reviewed all 34 files in the assigned workflow-multibranch source snapshot, with close reading of all 13 Java files (no test sources present). The strongest source-evidence lead is in JobPropertyStep: the `properties` Pipeline step mutates the current job's JobProperty set (add/remove) with no authorization check whatsoever. This directly bypasses the explicit job-ACL restriction implemented in BranchJobProperty.decorateACL, which denies Item.CONFIGURE and (for non-dead branches) Item.DELETE on multibranch branch projects. Other reviewed areas (ReadTrustedStep trust comparison and workspace path containment, SCMBinder trusted-revision selection, SCMVar `scm` resolution, ResolveScmStep JSON binding, durability/branch properties, project factories) were either consistent with intended trust boundaries or yielded only unconfirmed, lower-impact leads. This is a lead requiring runtime/design confirmation, not a confirmed vulnerability; no code was executed and no external references were consulted.
